2819.title: Sprint Review
2819.heading: Sprint Review
2819.content:
The Sprint Review is an inspection of the working [[Product Increment]] by the Scrum Team and relevant stakeholders. In game development, participants play or observe the game, discuss what changed, and use the result to adapt the Product Backlog.

Acceptance is based on demonstrated behavior and the applicable [[Definition of Done]], not on reports that component tasks are nearly complete.

2822.title: Sprite
2822.heading: Sprite
2822.content:
A sprite is a two-dimensional image rendered as a discrete game object or visual element. Its texture, position, scale, orientation, and drawing order determine how it appears in the scene.

Animated sprites select successive source images over time, often from a [[Sprite Sheet]]. Sprites remain the primary visual building block of many 2D games even though modern displays and assets are much larger than their early counterparts.

2825.title: Sprite Sheet
2825.heading: Sprite Sheet
2825.content:
A sprite sheet packs multiple sprite images or animation frames into one larger texture. Rendering selects a rectangular region of that texture rather than loading a separate image for every pose.

Packing reduces texture changes and keeps related frames together. [[Sprite Animation]] advances the selected region according to its own timing rather than assuming one animation image per rendered frame.

2827.sourceSearchName: sprite particle rendering sprite particle rendering
2827.title: Sprite Particle Rendering
2827.heading: Document

2828.sourceSearchName: sprite particle rendering sprite particle rendering
2828.title: Sprite Particle Rendering
2828.heading: Sprite Particle Rendering
2828.content: Instead of rendering heavy volumes for every particle, an image or footage sprite can be attached to each simulated point. The book uses cloud-image sprites on a fountain-like particle path to make rocket exhaust and a spiraling missile trail. Their speed and visual detail make them useful when the camera view preserves the billboard illusion. A camera move that reveals the cards' flatness or an effect whose debris must spin in volume needs [[Geometry-Instanced Particle Debris]] instead.

2829.sourceSearchName: sprite particle rendering sprite particle rendering
2829.title: Sprite Particle Rendering
2829.heading: References

2831.title: Sprite Component
2831.heading: Sprite Component
2831.content:
A sprite component attaches a two-dimensional image and drawing behavior to a [[Game Actor]]. It derives its position, scale, and rotation from the actor while storing presentation-specific data such as texture, dimensions, and draw order.

The renderer maintains sprite components in sorted order so the [[2D Painter's Algorithm]] produces the intended layering. An animated specialization can change texture regions over time without altering the actor model.

2834.title: Sprite Animation
2834.heading: Sprite Animation
2834.content:
Sprite animation presents a timed sequence of sprite images so a two-dimensional object appears to move or change. The current frame is commonly chosen from a [[Sprite Sheet]].

Animation speed should be stored independently from the rendering frame rate. Elapsed game time can advance the animation at its intended frames per second even when display performance varies.

2837.title: Sprint
2837.heading: Sprint
2837.content:
A Sprint is a fixed one-to-three-week interval in which a [[Scrum Team]] pursues a [[Sprint Goal]] and produces a usable [[Product Increment]]. Its stable duration creates a regular opportunity to inspect the product and adapt both plans and practices.

A Sprint contains planning, daily coordination, development, review, and retrospective work. It is not merely a deadline for a batch of disconnected tasks.

2840.title: Sprint Retrospective
2840.heading: Sprint Retrospective
2840.content:
A Sprint Retrospective inspects how a team created value and identifies a small improvement to try in the next Sprint. A simple format asks what to stop, start, and continue, then assigns and tracks the chosen action.

The event focuses on the working system, relationships, tools, and practices. It turns [[Continuous Improvement]] into an explicit recurring responsibility.

2843.title: Sprint Planning
2843.heading: Sprint Planning
2843.content:
Sprint Planning establishes a [[Sprint Goal]], selects feasible [[Product Backlog Item|Product Backlog Items]], and creates an initial plan for delivering them. The Product Owner clarifies value and priorities while the Development Team determines what it can accomplish and how.

The plan is a forecast based on capacity and past results. It can be adapted during the Sprint as long as the goal remains viable.

2846.title: Sprint Reset
2846.heading: Sprint Reset
2846.content:
A Sprint reset ends and replans a Sprint when its goal has become obsolete or impossible. Incomplete backlog items return to the Product Backlog and the team begins planning again from the changed reality.

A reset is deliberately rare because it discards coordination and creates overhead. Ordinary discovery should be handled by adapting the Sprint plan while preserving the goal.

2849.title: Sprint Goal
2849.heading: Sprint Goal
2849.content:
A Sprint Goal is the coherent outcome a team intends to achieve during a [[Sprint]]. It gives the selected backlog work a shared purpose and supports trade-offs when details change.

For a game team, a strong goal describes playable value or the reduction of an important risk. Completing unrelated discipline tasks is weaker because it postpones integration and obscures whether the player experience improved.

2852.title: Sprint Backlog
2852.heading: Sprint Backlog
2852.content:
The Sprint Backlog is the selected set of [[Product Backlog Item|Product Backlog Items]] and the team's evolving plan for meeting the [[Sprint Goal]]. It makes the current work visible and belongs to the Development Team.

As knowledge changes during the Sprint, tasks and implementation details can change. The backlog is therefore a live coordination artifact rather than a contract frozen at planning.

2854.sourceSearchName: spring follow camera spring follow camera
2854.title: Spring Follow Camera
2854.heading: Document

2855.sourceSearchName: spring follow camera spring follow camera
2855.title: Spring Follow Camera
2855.heading: Spring Follow Camera
2855.content:
A spring follow camera treats the desired follow position as an anchor connected to the actual camera by a damped spring. Displacement creates a restoring force, while damping reduces oscillation.

The resulting lag smooths sudden target motion and can make the view feel more natural than a rigid [[Follow Camera]]. Spring constants and damping must be tuned so responsiveness is preserved without jitter or prolonged overshoot.

2858.heading: Spline Handle Choice for Rotoscopy
2858.content: Spline type affects how a roto contour bends between control points. A Bezier spline can hold a sharp change of direction through its handles, while a B-spline tends to produce a smoother curve with tension distributed across neighboring points. A smooth contour with unnecessarily many points becomes difficult to animate and may wobble. The best choice follows the subject's actual silhouette rather than a habit of adding vertices. See [[Segmenting Moving Roto Shapes]] for why separate shapes also reduce contour complexity.

2861.heading: Split Exact Sequence
2861.content:
A [[Short Exact Sequence]] 0 → A → B → C → 0 splits when the surjection B → C has a right inverse C → B. Equivalently, the injection A → B has a compatible left inverse.

Splitting produces an isomorphism B ≅ A ⊕ C. Projective modules force sequences ending in them to split, while injective modules force sequences beginning in them to split.

2864.heading: Split-Complementary Color Balance
2864.content:
A split-complementary scheme begins with one base hue and replaces its direct complement with the two hues adjacent to that complement. It preserves noticeable contrast while distributing it across a less confrontational relationship.

The base hue can establish the environmental field while the two opposing hues separate different accents or gameplay categories. Value and saturation control keep the three colors hierarchical instead of equally dominant.

2867.title: Spline Camera
2867.heading: Spline Camera
2867.content:
A spline camera moves along a smooth curve defined by control points. It is useful for cutscenes, introductions, and guided views where authored motion should pass through a sequence of locations without sharp corners.

Position can be evaluated from a [[Catmull-Rom Spline]], while orientation may follow a separate target or interpolated path. Timing determines how quickly the camera traverses each curve segment.

2870.title: Spiking Neuron
2870.heading: Spiking Neuron
2870.content:
A spiking neuron maintains an internal activation potential that changes as input pulses arrive and decays when they do not. It emits an output event only when the potential crosses a threshold. Timing therefore matters: enough inputs must occur within a suitable window to trigger a spike.

Kelleher contrasts this event-driven unit with a standard artificial neuron that computes an activation from the inputs at each processing step. In [[Neuromorphic Computing]], sparse firing can reduce repeated activity and energy use. It is a hardware-oriented computational model inspired by biological signaling, not a claim that all neural-network tasks are better expressed with spikes.

2873.title: Spike
2873.heading: Spike
2873.content:
A spike is a timeboxed backlog item whose primary result is knowledge. A team uses it to research, experiment, or prototype when uncertainty prevents responsible estimation or design.

The spike answers a stated question and ends at its time limit. Any production feature revealed by the work is planned separately, preventing investigation from silently becoming unbounded implementation.

2876.title: Spherical Law of Sines
2876.heading: Spherical Law of Sines
2876.content:
For a spherical triangle,

$$\frac{\sin a}{\sin A}=\frac{\sin b}{\sin B}=\frac{\sin c}{\sin C}.$$

Lowercase letters denote angular side lengths and uppercase letters the opposite vertex angles. Like the plane [[Law of Sines]], the relation connects opposite parts, but all six quantities here are angles.

2879.title: Spherical Triangle
2879.heading: Spherical Triangle
2879.content: A spherical triangle is a region on a sphere bounded by three arcs of [[Great Circle]]s. Its side lengths are measured as central angles, and its vertex angles are angles between the corresponding great-circle planes. Unlike a Euclidean triangle, its interior-angle sum is greater than $180^\circ$.

2882.heading: Spherical Law of Cosines
2882.content:
For a unit-sphere triangle with side lengths $a,b,c$ opposite angles $A,B,C$, the spherical law of cosines is

$$\cos c=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\cos C.$$

It replaces the plane [[Law of Cosines]] when the triangle's sides are great-circle arcs and solves spherical side-angle relationships.

2885.heading: Sphere-AABB Intersection
2885.content:
A sphere-AABB intersection test finds the point on an axis-aligned box closest to the sphere center by clamping each coordinate to the box interval. The sphere intersects when the squared distance to that closest point is no greater than the squared radius.

This reduces a mixed-shape test to [[Point-in-AABB Test|clamping]] plus a distance comparison. It also supplies a useful closest point for later response calculations.

2888.heading: Speech-to-Text Service
2888.content:
A speech-to-text service exposes [[Automatic Speech Recognition]] through a network interface. A device sends captured audio to a remote system and receives a transcript that another assistant component can interpret.

Centralized services can use large models and compute resources, but they introduce latency, connectivity, and privacy concerns. Local [[Wake Word]] detection can limit transmission to audio that follows a likely activation.

Sphere Projection maps vertices according to their angular position around a spherical center. It provides a natural starting layout for globes, balls, domes, and other rounded assets.

Like a geographic map, the projection introduces distortion near its poles and requires a longitudinal cut. Rotating the mesh or projection direction can move those problem areas to less visible parts of the asset before island cleanup.

2894.title: Sphere Equation
2894.heading: Sphere Equation
2894.content:
A sphere with center $(h,k,l)$ and radius $r$ is the set of points satisfying

$$(x-h)^2+(y-k)^2+(z-l)^2=r^2.$$

The equation fixes the three-dimensional distance from every surface point to the center, extending the planar [[Circle Equation]] by one coordinate.

2897.title: Speech Synthesizer
2897.heading: Speech Synthesizer
2897.content:
A speech synthesizer generates the acoustic waveform for a planned sequence of speech sounds and prosodic targets. It may concatenate recorded units, predict acoustic parameters, or generate audio directly with a neural model.

The synthesizer is the final computational stage of [[Text-to-Speech]] before digital-to-analog conversion and playback. Its output quality depends on the linguistic and prosodic information supplied upstream.

2899.sourceSearchName: speech recognizer training speech recognizer training

2900.sourceSearchName: speech recognizer training speech recognizer training
2900.title: Speech Recognizer Training
2900.heading: Speech Recognizer Training
2900.content:
Speech recognizer training estimates model parameters from recorded utterances paired with transcriptions. Effective data include many speakers, accents, devices, noise conditions, and speaking styles relevant to the intended use.

The transcript provides word labels, while the audio supplies acoustic evidence. Coverage matters because a recognizer cannot reliably learn variation missing from its [[Training Dataset]].

2901.sourceSearchName: speech recognizer training speech recognizer training

2902.title: Speech Recognition Search

2903.sourceSearchName: speech recognition search speech recognition search
2903.title: Speech Recognition Search
2903.heading: Speech Recognition Search
2903.content:
Speech recognition search finds the most plausible word sequence given acoustic evidence, pronunciations, and language probabilities. It must compare many hypotheses without exhaustively enumerating every possible sentence.

The search balances how well a sequence fits the [[Acoustic Model]] with how plausible it is under the [[Statistical Language Model]], using the [[Pronunciation Model]] to connect words to sound units.

2906.title: Speech Recognition Grammar
2906.heading: Speech Recognition Grammar
2906.content:
A speech recognition grammar specifies the words and phrase patterns a recognizer should consider in a constrained interaction. Restricting the search space can improve accuracy when the next valid responses are predictable.

A [[Directed Prompt]] can establish such expectations for the user and system. Broad assistants need more open statistical models because their possible utterances cannot be enumerated compactly.

2909.title: Speech Frame
2909.heading: Speech Frame
2909.content:
A speech frame is a short segment of audio treated as approximately stable for acoustic analysis. Speech recognizers commonly analyze overlapping intervals on the order of about ten milliseconds.

Each frame is transformed by [[Speech Feature Extraction]] into measurements such as filter-bank energies. A sequence of frames lets an [[Acoustic Model]] track how speech evolves over time.

2911.sourceSearchName: speech feature extraction speech feature extraction
2911.title: Speech Feature Extraction
2911.heading: Document

2912.sourceSearchName: speech feature extraction speech feature extraction
2912.title: Speech Feature Extraction
2912.heading: Speech Feature Extraction
2912.content:
Speech feature extraction converts a digitized audio signal into a sequence of compact measurements suited to recognition. It divides speech into short [[Speech Frame|frames]] and summarizes the spectral energy in each interval.

The result is a sequence of [[Feature Vector|feature vectors]] that preserves information useful for distinguishing sounds while discarding much of the raw waveform's size and irrelevant detail.

2915.sourceSearchName: spectrum of a ring spectrum of a ring
2915.title: Spectrum of a Ring
2915.heading: Spectrum of a Ring
2915.content:
The spectrum Spec(R) of a ring R is the set of its [[Prime Ideal]]s equipped with the [[Zariski Topology]]. Closed subsets have the form V(I), consisting of primes that contain an ideal I.

The spectrum treats prime ideals as generalized points. Pairing it with the [[Structure Sheaf]] produces an [[Affine Scheme]], whose local rings encode algebra near each prime.

2918.title: Spectral Radius
2918.heading: Spectral Radius
2918.content:
The spectral radius of a square matrix is the largest absolute value among its eigenvalues: $\rho(A)=\max_i|\lambda_i|$.

For an [[Iteration Matrix]] $T$, the linear iteration converges from any initial vector exactly when $\rho(T)<1$. The quantity also connects matrix powers with the long-run growth or decay of repeated transformations.

2921.content:
Spectral feature selection evaluates attributes by how well they preserve the structure encoded in a similarity graph. Eigenvectors of a graph operator provide soft indicators of important geometric or cluster relationships, and features are scored against those indicators.

The approach can detect nonlinear structure that a global variance score misses. Its conclusions depend on how the graph, edge weights, neighborhood scale, and number of spectral components are chosen.

2927.heading: Specific Latent Heat
2927.content: Specific latent heat is the energy per unit mass required for a phase change at constant temperature. The transfer is $Q=mL$. Latent heat of fusion applies between solid and liquid, while latent heat of vaporization applies between liquid and gas. Energy changes molecular arrangement rather than average kinetic energy during the transition.

2930.heading: Specific Heat Capacity
2930.content: Specific heat capacity is the energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram of a material by one kelvin. For a temperature change without phase change, $Q=mc\Delta T$. The property is material-dependent, so equal masses receiving equal energy can undergo different temperature changes.

2933.title: Special Relativity
2933.heading: Special Relativity
2933.content: Special relativity rests on two postulates: the laws of physics have the same form in every inertial frame, and light in vacuum has the same speed for every inertial observer. Space and time coordinates therefore depend on relative motion, while the spacetime interval remains invariant. The theory replaces Galilean transformations with Lorentz transformations.

2936.title: Special Factorization
2936.heading: Special Factorization
2936.content:
A special factorization recognizes a polynomial as one side of a standard algebraic identity. Common patterns include a difference of squares, a perfect-square trinomial, and sums or differences of cubes.

Recognition can shorten work and reveal further factors. For example,

$$x^4-81=(x^2-9)(x^2+9)=(x-3)(x+3)(x^2+9).$$

The first identity exposes another difference of squares, so factorization continues in stages. A pattern should be verified against all signs and exponents rather than applied from visual resemblance alone.

2939.heading: Spearman Rank Correlation
2939.content:
Spearman rank correlation computes a correlation after replacing measurements with their ranks. It measures monotonic association and reduces the leverage of an extreme magnitude because only the observation's order is retained.

The statistic is useful when a [[Pearson Correlation Coefficient]] is dominated by outliers or when a relationship is monotonic but not well summarized as linear. Ranking also discards distance information, so the two coefficients answer different questions.

2942.title: Speaker-Independent Recognition
2942.heading: Speaker-Independent Recognition
2942.content:
Speaker-independent recognition is designed to transcribe speech from people who were not individually enrolled with the system. Training must cover a broad range of voices, accents, ages, speaking styles, and recording conditions.

This breadth makes the task harder than [[Speaker-Dependent Recognition]]. Its success depends strongly on a representative [[Training Dataset]] and an [[Acoustic Model]] able to generalize across speakers.

2943.sourceSearchName: speaker independent recognition speaker independent recognition

2944.sourceSearchName: speaker dependent recognition speaker dependent recognition

2945.sourceSearchName: speaker dependent recognition speaker dependent recognition
2945.title: Speaker-Dependent Recognition
2945.heading: Speaker-Dependent Recognition
2945.content:
Speaker-dependent recognition is trained or adapted for a particular person's voice. Because the system can specialize to one speaker's pronunciation and vocal characteristics, it may recognize a limited vocabulary more accurately with less general data.

The specialization is a constraint: performance may fall sharply for other users. [[Speaker-Independent Recognition]] instead aims to cover variation across many speakers.

2948.content: A spatiotemporal time-series plot draws a separate temporal trajectory for each spatial location or zone in a shared panel or aligned set of panels. It emphasizes timing, common peaks, and persistent differences but removes map position. Thin transparent lines can reveal the network's overall behavior. A [[Space-Time XT Plot]] may make long-duration level differences easier to scan, while maps identify where those locations are.

2951.title: Spatiotemporal Point Symbol
2951.heading: Spatiotemporal Point Symbol
2951.content: A spatiotemporal point symbol represents a location's value at one time through size, color, or both. Repeating the mapping across panels or animation lets the same station be followed through time. Size should use area-based scaling, and color classes must remain stable across frames. If both channels encode the same value, redundancy can reinforce magnitude; if they encode different variables, the legend must explain their combination.

2954.title: Spatiotemporal Data
2954.heading: Spatiotemporal Data
2954.content: Spatiotemporal data associate observations with both geographic positions and times. Their structure depends on which combinations exist: every feature may be observed at every time in a [[Full Space-Time Grid]], only selected lattice combinations may appear in a [[Sparse Space-Time Grid]], measurements may be irregular, or positions may form trajectories. Visualization must decide whether to preserve space, time, or both in each view.

2957.title: Spatio-Temporal-Thematic Social Analysis
2957.heading: Spatio-Temporal-Thematic Social Analysis
2957.content:
Spatio-temporal-thematic social analysis jointly examines what people discuss, where activity occurs, and how it changes over time. It integrates textual themes with geographic and temporal features rather than analyzing each dimension separately.

Systems such as Twitris organize these relationships for event and trend analysis. Coupled views can reveal localized emerging topics, but sampling bias and missing location data limit conclusions about the wider population.

2959.title: Spatially Varying Thermal Properties
2959.heading: Document

2960.sourceSearchName: spatially varying thermal properties spatially varying thermal properties
2960.title: Spatially Varying Thermal Properties
2960.heading: Spatially Varying Thermal Properties
2960.content:
Thermophysical properties can vary by domain, direction, or location within one geometry. A conductivity defined as $k(x,y,z)$ represents a continuously inhomogeneous material, while separate domain assignments represent distinct layers or components.

Spatial variation must correspond to the model's coordinate system and selections. It can create localized gradients even under simple boundary conditions, making [[COMSOL Domain and Boundary Selections|correct entity assignment]] and targeted mesh refinement essential.

2961.title: Spatially Varying Thermal Properties
2961.heading: References

2963.title: Spatial Trajectory
2963.heading: Spatial Trajectory
2963.content: A spatial trajectory is an ordered sequence of locations associated with successive times, representing the movement of an entity through space. Its position and time are linked rather than forming all possible combinations of independent spatial and temporal indexes. The `spacetime` package uses STT and [[STTDF Object|STTDF]] for simple trajectories. Speed or direction can be derived only after accounting for time intervals and the coordinate system.

2966.title: Spatial Tooltip
2966.heading: Spatial Tooltip
2966.content: A spatial tooltip displays a short attribute value or label when the pointer reaches a map feature. It provides detail on demand without permanently covering nearby points or regions. Because tooltips disappear, they are poorly suited to comparing many locations or communicating essential categories. Selection tolerance, touch support, and unambiguous feature highlighting help users understand which geometry supplied the displayed information.

2969.title: Spatial Resolution
2969.heading: Spatial Resolution
2969.content:
Spatial resolution describes how finely an [[Output Device]] can distinguish or present information across space.

For a [[Visual Display]], resolution depends on both pixel count and screen size rather than pixel count alone. Viewing distance also affects perceived resolution because individual pixels become less distinguishable at greater distances. For a [[Haptic Display]], spatial resolution is the minimum spatial separation between stimuli the device can present, which should be matched to the sensitivity of the body location being stimulated.

Higher resolution can improve detail, but its value depends on the user, task, viewing or contact conditions, and other parts of [[Display Fidelity]].

For a near-eye AR display, angular resolution describes how much visual angle each resolvable element occupies. Increasing pixel count without considering field of view, optics, and eye position does not by itself determine how finely registered details can be perceived.

2972.title: Spatial Registration
2972.heading: Spatial Registration
2972.content:
Spatial registration aligns corresponding virtual and physical information within a shared geometric frame. A registered augmentation remains attached to its referenced object or location as the user changes viewpoint.

The alignment depends on tracking, calibrated camera and display relationships, object models, and the complete chain of coordinate transformations. Static calibration error and runtime measurement error appear directly as displacement between the virtual content and the physical target.

2974.sourceSearchName: spatial point data spatial point data
2974.title: Spatial Point Data
2974.heading: Document

2975.sourceSearchName: spatial point data spatial point data
2975.title: Spatial Point Data
2975.heading: Spatial Point Data
2975.content: Spatial point data represent features whose relevant location can be expressed by a coordinate pair at the map's scale. Stations, cities, and sampled observations are typical examples. Attributes attached to each point may be encoded by a [[Proportional Symbol Map]] or used as inputs to [[Point-Surface Interpolation]]. The coordinates are interpretable only with a [[Coordinate Reference System]] that states how they relate to the Earth.

2977.title: Spatial Polygon Data
2977.heading: Document

2978.sourceSearchName: spatial polygon data spatial polygon data
2978.title: Spatial Polygon Data
2978.heading: Spatial Polygon Data
2978.content: Spatial polygon data represent areas enclosed by one or more rings, possibly including holes or multiple disconnected parts. Administrative regions and land-cover zones are common examples. Polygon attributes can be encoded with a [[Choropleth Map]], which visually assumes a value applies throughout each region. Boundaries can also provide geographic context over a [[Quantitative Raster Map]].

2979.title: Spatial Polygon Data

2980.title: Spatial Point Labeling

2981.sourceSearchName: spatial point labeling spatial point labeling
2981.title: Spatial Point Labeling
2981.heading: Spatial Point Labeling
2981.content: Spatial point labeling places names or values near mapped locations while attempting to prevent collisions with symbols and other labels. Automated placement can search alternative positions around a point, but dense maps may still require prioritization or omission. Labels should attach unambiguously to their locations and remain subordinate to the quantitative encoding. Interactive [[Spatial Tooltip|tooltips]] offer an alternative when permanent labels would cover the map.

2983.title: Spatial Line Data
2983.heading: Document

2984.sourceSearchName: spatial line data spatial line data
2984.title: Spatial Line Data
2984.heading: Spatial Line Data
2984.content: Spatial line data represent extended features through ordered coordinate sequences. Roads, rivers, routes, and administrative boundaries can be stored as lines even though their physical width may be ignored at the chosen scale. Lines often supply context in a [[Map Layer Overlay]], but they can also carry attributes such as category or flow. Their geometry and other layers must use compatible coordinate reference systems.

2985.sourceSearchName: spatial line data spatial line data
2985.title: Spatial Line Data
2985.heading: References

2987.title: Spatial Knowledge
2987.heading: Spatial Knowledge
2987.content:
Spatial knowledge is remembered information about an environment and its arrangement. It forms a [[Cognitive Map]] and supports [[Wayfinding]].

Three important forms are:

- Landmark knowledge: visual characteristics and distinctive objects.
- Route knowledge: sequences of actions needed to follow paths between places.
- Survey knowledge: map-like knowledge of locations, distances, orientations, and topology.

People often begin with landmark information, learn routes between landmarks, and gradually develop survey knowledge. Travel methods, viewpoints, maps, and [[Reference Frame]]s can change which forms are acquired and how easily they are used.

2990.title: Spatial Field
2990.heading: Spatial Field
2990.content: A spatial field treats a variable as potentially defined at every location in a region, even when it is observed only at a finite set of samples. Elevation, temperature, and solar radiation are common examples. A raster discretizes the field into cells as [[Raster Data]], while [[Point-Surface Interpolation]] estimates unsampled locations from point observations. Field maps emphasize spatial pattern rather than individual named objects.

2993.title: Spatial Distortion
2993.heading: Spatial Distortion
2993.content:
Spatial distortion deliberately bends, compresses, or displaces parts of a represented scene to reveal otherwise occluded information. Unlike a physically faithful view, it sacrifices local geometric accuracy to preserve access to both the target and its context.

The deformation should remain understandable and stable enough that users can relate the changed view back to the physical environment. Smooth transitions can help communicate how the distorted arrangement was derived.

2996.title: Spatial Dimensionality in Thermal Models
2996.heading: Spatial Dimensionality in Thermal Models
2996.content:
Heat-transfer geometry may be expressed in one, two, or three Cartesian dimensions, or in cylindrical and spherical coordinates when those systems match the shape. The chosen dimensionality determines which temperature gradients and heat-flux components the model can represent.

A lower-dimensional approximation is justified when variation in an omitted direction is negligible compared with the dominant heat-flow directions. This physical argument, not computational convenience alone, is the basis of [[Geometry Dimensionality Reduction|dimensionality reduction]].

2999.title: Spatial Feature
2999.heading: Spatial Feature
2999.content: A spatial feature is a geographic entity represented by geometry together with descriptive attributes. A feature may be a point, line, polygon, or a multipart collection of these forms. In the [[Simple Feature]] model, each row of a data frame represents one feature and a geometry list-column stores its shape. Mapping joins the feature's attributes to visual properties while its geometry determines position and extent.

3001.title: Spatial Augmented Reality
3001.heading: Document

3002.sourceSearchName: spatial augmented reality spatial augmented reality
3002.title: Spatial Augmented Reality
3002.heading: Spatial Augmented Reality
3002.content:
Spatial augmented reality places the display technology in the environment rather than carrying it on the user's head or body. Stationary screens or projectors present augmentations at fixed physical locations and can support several viewers without requiring each person to wear a display.

Projected forms place light directly on physical surfaces, making the object itself part of the display. Their usable geometry, brightness, shadows, and occlusion depend on the projector, object, user, and environmental arrangement.

3004.heading: Document

3005.sourceSearchName: spatial data reprojection spatial data reprojection
3005.title: Spatial Data Reprojection
3005.heading: Spatial Data Reprojection
3005.content: Spatial data reprojection transforms geometry coordinates from one [[Coordinate Reference System]] to another. It is necessary when layers use different datums or projections and must align in a [[Map Layer Overlay]]. The operation can distort distance, area, direction, or shape according to the destination projection, and rasters require resampling as well as coordinate transformation. The target system should therefore suit both the base map and the intended comparisons.

3006.sourceSearchName: spatial data reprojection spatial data reprojection
3006.title: Spatial Data Reprojection
3006.heading: References

3008.title: Spatial Data
3008.heading: Spatial Data
3008.content: Spatial data associate observations with locations or geographic geometries and a [[Coordinate Reference System]]. The source distinguishes discrete objects, represented through [[Spatial Point Data|points]], lines, or polygons, from continuous [[Spatial Field|fields]], commonly represented as rasters. This distinction influences storage, analysis, and visualization: objects have identifiable boundaries or paths, while fields assign a potential value throughout a region.

3011.title: Spatial Audio
3011.heading: Spatial Audio
3011.content:
Spatial audio presents sound so that it appears to originate from a location or direction in three-dimensional space. It uses the listener's auditory localization abilities to provide an aural sense of the environment.

One approach records separate left- and right-ear signals in a real setting. Another filters a monaural source through head-related transfer functions for a desired location, which supports interactive placement but must address individual differences and missing reverberation. [[Auralization]] instead models how sound propagates and reflects through an environment.

Spatial audio can support [[Wayfinding]], reveal off-screen events, and strengthen [[Presence]].

3013.sourceSearchName: spatial aggregation by zone spatial aggregation by zone
3013.title: Spatial Aggregation by Zone
3013.heading: Document

3014.sourceSearchName: spatial aggregation by zone spatial aggregation by zone
3014.title: Spatial Aggregation by Zone
3014.heading: Spatial Aggregation by Zone
3014.content: Spatial aggregation by zone reduces a raster layer to summaries over geographic bands or other regions. Repeating the operation through time turns a three-dimensional [[Space-Time Raster]] into a matrix whose rows or columns represent zones and times. The direction and summary function determine which pattern survives. Latitude means, for example, conceal longitudinal variation but can expose broad seasonal gradients.

3017.title: Sparsity-Based Feature Selection
3017.heading: Sparsity-Based Feature Selection
3017.content:
Sparsity-based feature selection adds a constraint or penalty that drives many model coefficients to zero. The remaining nonzero dimensions form an embedded feature subset.

Sparse objectives combine prediction and selection in one optimization problem and can scale better than explicit subset enumeration. Correlated inputs, penalty strength, and grouped structure influence which variables survive.

3020.title: Sparse Space-Time Grid
3020.heading: Sparse Space-Time Grid
3020.content: A sparse space-time grid stores only the non-missing combinations from an underlying lattice of spatial features and observation times. It avoids allocating every cell of a [[Full Space-Time Grid]] when many combinations are absent while retaining the idea of shared spatial and temporal indexes. In the `spacetime` package, STS and [[STSDF Object|STSDF]] represent this layout.

3023.title: Sparse Model Matrix
3023.heading: Sparse Model Matrix
3023.content:
A sparse model matrix represents predictors numerically while storing only nonzero entries. It is efficient for one-hot encoded categorical data because most indicator columns are zero for any record.

The encoding rules must be learned from training data and applied consistently to validation, test, and future scoring records.

3026.title: Sparse Matrix
3026.heading: Sparse Matrix
3026.content:
A sparse matrix is a [[Matrix]] in which most entries are zero. Instead of reserving memory for every position, an implementation can store only the coordinates and values of nonzero entries.

The web's [[Hyperlink Matrix]] is sparse because each page links to only a tiny fraction of all pages. Exploiting that structure makes calculations over a graph containing billions of nodes far more practical in time and storage.

3029.title: Sparse Rotospline Keyframing
3029.heading: Sparse Rotospline Keyframing
3029.content: Rotoscopy does not need a new hand-shaped outline on every frame. Place keyframes at important motion changes or extrema, let the spline interpolate between them, and inspect the resulting edge. Whole-shape translation or rotation can handle motion that does not require reshaping. Too many independently adjusted keyframes may make the contour chatter, while too few may let it drift away from the subject. The method works best after the subject is divided into manageable pieces as in [[Segmenting Moving Roto Shapes]].

3032.sourceSearchName: sparse document vector clustering sparse document vector clustering
3032.title: Sparse Document Vector Clustering
3032.heading: Sparse Document Vector Clustering
3032.content:
A sparse document vector represents a text using weights for only the terms that occur, commonly after frequency and inverse-document-frequency transformations. Most vocabulary coordinates are zero, making sparse storage and computation essential.

Cosine-like similarity often focuses on term distribution rather than document magnitude. High dimensionality, synonymy, polysemy, and common background language can still obscure the topical structure sought by clustering.

3035.sourceSearchName: sparse clustering feature selection sparse clustering feature selection
3035.title: Sparse Clustering Feature Selection
3035.heading: Sparse Clustering Feature Selection
3035.content:
Sparse clustering attaches weights to features and penalizes those weights so that many become exactly zero. Clustering and feature selection are then solved together: dimensions that do not help the partition lose influence.

Sparsity improves interpretability and can protect distances from irrelevant dimensions. The penalty level controls the selected set, and an overly strong penalty can erase weak features whose value appears only through interaction with others.

3038.title: Sparse Autoencoder
3038.heading: Sparse Autoencoder
3038.content:
A sparse autoencoder adds a constraint that encourages only a small proportion of hidden units to be active for any input. The network may therefore use a wide hidden layer without learning a trivial identity representation.

Sparse activation promotes selective, parts-like features and can improve interpretability. The strength and form of the sparsity penalty determine the balance between accurate reconstruction and specialized codes.

3041.title: Span
3041.heading: Span
3041.content:
The span of a set of vectors is the collection of all their [[Linear Combination|linear combinations]]. It is the smallest [[Vector Subspace]] containing those vectors.

A set spans a vector space when every vector in the space can be expressed from it. A spanning set that is also linearly independent is a [[Basis]].

3044.title: Spark SQL
3044.heading: Spark SQL
3044.content:
Spark SQL compiles relational queries into operations executed by the Spark runtime. In the book's described version, it reused Hive parsing and metastore compatibility while using its own Catalyst logical optimizer and DataFrame representation.

In-memory reusable data reduces disk input/output and job-restart overhead when queries feed iterative analysis. The account is version-specific and notes that contemporary Spark SQL supported only a subset of HiveQL features.

3047.heading: Space-Wide Time Series
3047.content: A space-wide time series stores each spatial zone or location as a separate variable and each time as a shared observation row. It converts a space-time dataset into a multivariate temporal form, enabling conventional line and horizon plots. The representation preserves temporal comparison among locations but treats geographic adjacency as metadata rather than visible position. Maps are needed to restore that spatial relationship.

3050.title: Space-Wide Point Time Series
3050.heading: Space-Wide Point Time Series
3050.content: A space-wide point time series uses time as the row index and gives each point location its own value column. It is created by reshaping [[Long-Format Space-Time Data]] and supports multivariate temporal plotting. To construct a full point space-time object, its values can be transposed and vectorized so the spatial index varies fastest within each time. The wide form makes missing location-time combinations explicit.

3053.title: Space-Time Raster
3053.heading: Space-Time Raster
3053.content: A space-time raster is a sequence of aligned raster layers whose cells describe a field at successive times. It forms a three-dimensional array with two spatial dimensions and one temporal dimension. A [[Space-Time Level Plot]] shows selected snapshots, while [[Hovmoller Diagram|Hovmoller diagrams]] or time-series reductions aggregate one spatial direction. No single two-dimensional display preserves every relationship in the full array.

3056.title: Space-Time XT Plot
3056.heading: Space-Time XT Plot
3056.content: A space-time XT plot places spatial locations or zones on the horizontal axis, time on the vertical axis, and observed value in color. Each column traces one location through time, enabling comparison of persistent levels and shared temporal events across a network. The display preserves the location identities but not their two-dimensional geographic arrangement, so a [[Space-Time Map Series]] supplies complementary spatial context.

3059.title: Space-Time Raster Violin Plot
3059.heading: Space-Time Raster Violin Plot
3059.content: A space-time raster violin plot combines a density-shaped silhouette with box-plot summaries for the cells belonging to each temporal group. It reveals changes in central tendency, spread, and multimodality, such as recurring clear-sky and overcast modes. The shape depends on density bandwidth and ignores cell locations. [[Space-Time Raster Small Multiples]] are therefore needed to connect the distribution back to geography.

3062.heading: Space-Time Raster Small Multiples
3062.content: Space-time raster small multiples arrange a sequence of map snapshots in a regular panel grid. A fixed extent, color scale, and panel design let viewers compare both location and time by scanning corresponding cells. They are especially effective after [[Monthly Raster Aggregation]]. The number of panels must remain small enough to preserve spatial detail, and labels should make temporal order unmistakable.

3065.title: Space-Time Raster Histogram
3065.heading: Space-Time Raster Histogram
3065.content: A space-time raster histogram groups cell values by a time-derived condition and displays their frequency distributions in separate panels. Monthly histograms can reveal seasonal shifts, spread, skewness, or multiple modes that maps alone do not summarize. Because cells are pooled across geography, the display loses location. It therefore complements [[Space-Time Raster Small Multiples]] rather than explaining where each part of the distribution occurs.

3068.heading: Space-Time Raster Scatterplot Matrix
3068.content: A space-time raster scatterplot matrix compares cell values between every pair of selected raster times or temporal aggregates. Each point represents the same cell in two layers, so linear or nonlinear patterns show how spatial values persist or change. Diagonal density summaries describe each layer's distribution. The matrix grows quickly with layer count and does not show where deviating cells are located.

3071.title: Space-Time Raster Density Plot
3071.heading: Space-Time Raster Density Plot
3071.content: A space-time raster density plot estimates a smooth distribution of cell values for each selected temporal group. It can make multiple modes and gradual distribution changes easier to compare than a binned histogram. Bandwidth controls smoothness and can create or erase apparent structure. Since the plot aggregates across cells, it should be read alongside maps that preserve the geography of the [[Space-Time Raster]].
